## 9. Applications and discussion

**Topology.** The universal coefficient theorem is the standard tool for translating between integral homology and homology with arbitrary coefficients. Theorem 7.1 explains the well-known simplification in the rational case: rational homology is the "torsion-free shadow" of integral homology, and Betti numbers are all one can see. Theorem 7.5 explains why mod-$p$ homology sees strictly more: the $\operatorname{Tor}$-term promotes $p$-torsion in $H_{n-1}$ to a genuine class in $H_n(-;\mathbb{Z}/p)$. The classical example is $\mathbb{RP}^2$ (Remark 7.6).

**Group theory and extension problems.** By Remark 5.9, $\operatorname{Ext}^1(C,A)$ classifies abelian extensions. Corollary 5.7 says $\mathbb{Q}$ absorbs cyclic quotients trivially; Corollary 5.8 gives exactly $k$ inequivalent extensions of $\mathbb{Z}/k$ by $\mathbb{Z}$, realised as $0 \to \mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{k}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/k\to 0$ and its multiples. More generally Theorem 5.5 says that the extension classes of $\mathbb{Z}/k$ by $Y$ are parametrised by $Y/kY$, an entirely explicit finite computation whenever $Y$ is finitely generated.

**Commutative algebra.** Theorem 6.7 is the archetype of a *homological characterisation of a ring-theoretic property*: an infinite condition (exactness of $-\otimes G$ against all injections) collapses to a finite family of $\operatorname{Tor}$ computations against cyclic modules. The general form of this phenomenon is the standard flatness criterion "$\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(G, R/I) = 0$ for all finitely generated ideals $I$", of which our (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(4) is the case $R = \mathbb{Z}$, where every ideal is $k\mathbb{Z}$.

**The hereditary phenomenon.** Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 4.6, 6.5 all say the same thing from different angles: over $\mathbb{Z}$ the derived functors live in degrees $0$ and $1$ only. This is the defining property of a **hereditary ring** (global dimension $\leq 1$), which for a commutative domain is equivalent to being a Dedekind domain. Everything in this paper generalises verbatim to Dedekind domains, with $\mathbb{Z}/k$ replaced by $R/\mathfrak{a}$ and "$k$-divisible" by "$\mathfrak{a}$-divisible".

**What is genuinely explicit here.** Two aspects of the development deserve emphasis. First, the isomorphism $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,Y)\cong Y/kY$ is not obtained by an abstract dimension count but from a *named* surjection $y \mapsto \varepsilon\circ u_y$ whose kernel is computed exactly (Theorems 5.3, 5.4). One can therefore point at a specific extension realising any given class. Second, the two-term complex $C^{(k)}$ isolates the two extreme cases of the universal coefficient sequence in a single object: degree $0$ is pure tensor, degree $1$ is pure $\operatorname{Tor}$. This gives the shortest possible proof that the correction term is unavoidable.

**Limitations.** Theorem 4.6 covers finitely generated $X$; the fully general statement "$\operatorname{Ext}^{n}(X,Y)=0$ for all $n\ge 2$ and all abelian groups $X,Y$" requires the freeness of arbitrary (possibly uncountable) subgroups of free abelian groups (Remark 4.7). Theorems 7.3 and 7.4 establish the two extreme cases of the universal coefficient sequence for the specific complex $C^{(k)}$; the full short exact sequence, with its non-canonical splitting, for an arbitrary complex of free modules, is a natural next target.

---

## 10. Future directions

1. **Naturality of the degree-one computation.** Establish that $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k, Y) \cong Y/kY$ is natural in $Y$: for every homomorphism $f : Y \to Y'$ the square formed by the two isomorphisms, the induced map $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,f)$, and the map $Y/kY \to Y'/kY'$ induced by $f$, commutes. The isomorphism itself is Theorem 5.5, built from the explicit surjection $y \mapsto \varepsilon\circ u_y$ with kernel $kY$; what remains is functoriality of this description.

2. **Full hereditarity.** Prove $\operatorname{Ext}^{n+2}(X,Y) = 0$ for *all* abelian groups $X, Y$, removing the finite generation hypothesis of Theorem 4.6. The route is the Nielsen–Schreier-type theorem for abelian groups: every subgroup of a free abelian group is free, in arbitrary rank.

3. **The general universal coefficient sequence.** Construct the full short exact sequence $0 \to G\otimes H_n(C) \to H_n(G\otimes C)\to\operatorname{Tor}_1(G,H_{n-1}(C))\to 0$ for an arbitrary complex of free modules, and prove that it splits (non-canonically) and is natural in $C$ and $G$.

4. **Künneth.** Establish the Künneth formula $0 \to \bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(C)\otimes H_q(D)\to H_n(C\otimes D)\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\operatorname{Tor}_1(H_p(C),H_q(D))\to 0$, of which the universal coefficient theorem is the special case where $D$ is concentrated in degree zero.

5. **Cohomological universal coefficients.** The dual sequence $0 \to \operatorname{Ext}^1(H_{n-1}(C),G)\to H^n(C;G)\to\operatorname{Hom}(H_n(C),G)\to0$, which turns Section 5 into a topological tool exactly as Section 6 feeds Section 7.

6. **Dedekind and hereditary generalisations.** Reprove Sections 4–7 over an arbitrary Dedekind domain, with $\mathbb{Z}/k$ replaced by $R/\mathfrak{a}$, thereby covering rings of integers in number fields and coordinate rings of smooth affine curves.

7. **Beyond dimension one.** For a ring of global dimension $d > 1$ (e.g. a polynomial ring $\mathbb{k}[x_1,\dots,x_d]$, where the Koszul complex plays the role of $C^{(k)}$), compute the full tower $\operatorname{Ext}^0,\dots,\operatorname{Ext}^d$ against the residue field and observe the Betti numbers $\binom{d}{n}$ predicted by the Koszul resolution.

\begin{abstract}
We develop, from first principles and in complete detail, the homological algebra of the category of abelian groups, organised around two explicit length-one resolutions: the free resolution $0 \to \Z \xrightarrow{\cdot k} \Z \to \Z/k \to 0$ of a cyclic group, and the injective resolution $0 \to \Z \to \Q \to \Q/\Z \to 0$ of the integers. From these two sequences, together with the long exact sequence in homology attached to a short exact sequence of complexes, we obtain a self-contained account of the derived functors $\Ext^n$ and $\Tor_n$ over $\Z$.

Our main results are: (i) \emph{dimension bounds} --- $\Ext^{n}(\Z/k, Y) = 0$ and $\Tor_{n}(G, \Z/k) = 0$ for $n \geq 2$; $\Ext^{n}(X, \Z) = 0$ for $n \geq 2$ and all $X$; and $\Ext^{n}(X,Y) = 0$ for $n\ge 2$ whenever $X$ admits a projective presentation with projective kernel, in particular for every finitely generated abelian group $X$; (ii) \emph{explicit degree-one computations} --- an explicit surjection $Y \twoheadrightarrow \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)$ with kernel $kY$, giving $\Ext^1(\Z/k, Y) \cong Y/kY$, hence $\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)=0$ iff $Y$ is $k$-divisible, so $\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Q)=0$ while $\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Z)\cong\Z/k \ne 0$ for $k \ge 2$; dually $\Tor_1(G,\Z/k)\cong G[k]$ and $G\otimes\Z/k\cong G/kG$; (iii) a \emph{five-way flatness criterion} --- $G$ is flat iff torsion-free iff multiplication by every nonzero $k$ is injective iff $\Tor_1(G,\Z/k)=0$ for all $k\ne0$ iff all higher $\Tor$ vanish; in particular $\Z/k$ is not flat for $k\ge2$; and (iv) \emph{universal coefficients} --- for flat $G$, $H_n(G\otimes C)\cong G\otimes H_n(C)$ for every complex and every degree, and this fails for non-flat coefficients, as witnessed sharply by the two-term free complex $C = (\Z\xrightarrow{\cdot k}\Z)$, for which $H_0(G\otimes C)\cong G\otimes H_0(C)$ and $H_1(G\otimes C)\cong\Tor_1(G,H_0(C))$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Motivation}
The two fundamental constructions on modules --- the tensor product $-\otimes_R-$ and the hom-functor $\Hom_R(-,-)$ --- are not exact. Tensoring preserves cokernels but not kernels; $\Hom$ preserves kernels but not cokernels. Homological algebra is the systematic study of the resulting discrepancies. Rather than treating non-exactness as a defect, one constructs functors $\Tor_n$ and $\Ext^n$ measuring it, with $\Tor_0 = \otimes$, $\Ext^0 = \Hom$, and with any short exact sequence in either variable producing an infinite exact sequence linking all degrees.

Over the integers this programme reaches a particularly satisfying conclusion, because $\Z$ is a \emph{hereditary} ring: every submodule of a projective module is projective. Consequently all resolutions may be taken of length one, and the entire theory concentrates in degrees $0$ and $1$. This paper carries out that programme concretely, with all resolutions built by hand and all degree-one groups computed in closed form.

\subsection{Conventions}
All rings are unital; $R$ denotes a commutative ring. The unqualified word \emph{module} means $\Z$-module, i.e.\ abelian group. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a module $G$ we write
\[ G[k] := \{ g \in G : kg = 0 \}, \qquad kG := \{ kg : g \in G\}, \]
for the $k$-torsion subgroup and the subgroup of $k$-multiples. A module $Y$ is \emph{$k$-divisible} if $kY = Y$, and \emph{divisible} if $k$-divisible for all $k \geq 1$. Statements involving $\Z/k$ carry the standing hypothesis $k \neq 0$. Complexes are indexed over an arbitrary shape wherever possible.

\section{Good objects and explicit resolutions}

\subsection{Projective, injective, flat}

\begin{definition}
An $R$-module $P$ is \emph{projective} if $\Hom_R(P,-)$ is exact; equivalently, if every epimorphism onto $P$ splits; equivalently, if $P$ is a direct summand of a free module.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
An $R$-module $I$ is \emph{injective} if $\Hom_R(-,I)$ is exact; equivalently, if every homomorphism into $I$ defined on a submodule extends to the ambient module.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
An $R$-module $G$ is \emph{flat} if $G \otimes_R -$ is exact; as tensoring is always right exact, this amounts to $G\otimes_R-$ preserving injections.
\end{definition}

Over $\Z$ these notions have elementary descriptions. Projective $=$ free. Injective $=$ divisible, by Baer's criterion: it suffices to extend homomorphisms defined on the ideals $k\Z\subseteq\Z$, and such extensions exist exactly when the target is $k$-divisible for all $k$. Flat $=$ torsion-free (Theorem~\ref{thm:flat}).

\begin{example}\label{ex:div}
$\Q$ is divisible, hence an injective $\Z$-module; the quotient $\Q/\Z$ of a divisible group is divisible, hence also injective. The group $\Z$ is not divisible, hence not injective.
\end{example}

\subsection{The free resolution of a cyclic group}

\begin{theorem}[Standard free resolution of $\Z/k$]\label{thm:freeres}
Let $k \neq 0$, let $\mu_k : \Z\to\Z$ be multiplication by $k$ and $\pi_k : \Z\to\Z/k$ reduction. Then
\[ \mathcal{R}_k : \quad 0 \longrightarrow \Z \xrightarrow{\ \mu_k\ } \Z \xrightarrow{\ \pi_k\ } \Z/k \longrightarrow 0 \]
is a short exact sequence of $\Z$-modules whose two outer terms are free, hence projective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\pi_k\circ\mu_k = 0$ since $k\equiv 0 \bmod k$. If $ka = kb$ then $a = b$ because $\Z$ is a domain and $k\ne 0$, so $\mu_k$ is injective. Every residue class is the class of an integer, so $\pi_k$ is surjective. Finally $\pi_k(x)=0$ means $k \mid x$, i.e.\ $x \in \image\mu_k$.
\end{proof}

Placed as a chain complex concentrated in degrees $1$ and $0$,
\[ C^{(k)} : \quad \cdots \to 0 \to \Z \xrightarrow{\ \mu_k\ } \Z, \]
with augmentation $\pi_k$ in degree zero, this is a \emph{projective resolution} of $\Z/k$: the objects are free and $H_0(C^{(k)}) = \coker\mu_k = \Z/k$, $H_n(C^{(k)}) = 0$ for $n \geq 1$ (in degree $1$ because $\mu_k$ is injective, in higher degrees because the objects vanish).

\subsection{The injective resolution of $\Z$}

\begin{theorem}[Standard injective resolution of $\Z$]\label{thm:injres}
The sequence
\[ \mathcal{Q} : \quad 0 \longrightarrow \Z \xrightarrow{\ \iota\ } \Q \xrightarrow{\ p\ } \Q/\Z \longrightarrow 0, \]
with $\iota$ the inclusion and $p$ the quotient map, is short exact, and both $\Q$ and $\Q/\Z$ are injective $\Z$-modules.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\iota$ is injective, $p$ is surjective, and $p(x)=0$ iff $x\in\Z$. Injectivity of the terms is Example~\ref{ex:div}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:lengthone}
Both resolutions terminate after one step; this is the concrete manifestation of hereditarity of $\Z$. The principle we exploit repeatedly is: if $F$ is an additive functor and $M$ has a projective resolution $P_\bullet$ with $P_n = 0$ for $n\ge2$, then $(L_nF)(M) = H_n(F(P_\bullet)) = 0$ for $n\ge2$, since $F(0)=0$. Dually for right derived functors and injective resolutions.
\end{remark}

\section{The long exact sequence in homology}

Let $R$ be a ring, $c$ an arbitrary complex shape (covering chain and cochain complexes alike), and let $0 \to X_1 \xrightarrow{f} X_2 \xrightarrow{g} X_3 \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of complexes of $R$-modules.

\begin{theorem}[Long exact sequence]\label{thm:les}
There are connecting homomorphisms $\delta : H_i(X_3)\to H_j(X_1)$, defined whenever $j$ follows $i$ in the shape $c$, such that the following are exact at the indicated spots:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $H_i(X_1)\xrightarrow{H_i(f)} H_i(X_2)\xrightarrow{H_i(g)} H_i(X_3)$, exact at $H_i(X_2)$;
\item $H_i(X_2)\xrightarrow{H_i(g)} H_i(X_3)\xrightarrow{\delta} H_j(X_1)$, exact at $H_i(X_3)$;
\item $H_i(X_3)\xrightarrow{\delta} H_j(X_1)\xrightarrow{H_j(f)} H_j(X_2)$, exact at $H_j(X_1)$.
\end{enumerate}
Splicing yields $\cdots\to H_i(X_1)\to H_i(X_2)\to H_i(X_3)\xrightarrow{\delta} H_j(X_1)\to\cdots$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The connecting map is the classical snake chase: given a cycle $z$ of $X_3$, lift to $\tilde z \in X_2$ (possible since $g$ is degreewise surjective); then $g(d\tilde z) = dz = 0$, so $d\tilde z = f(w)$ for a unique cycle $w \in X_1$; set $\delta[z]:=[w]$. Independence of choices and the three exactness statements are verified by further chases. In the module setting all maps are honest $R$-linear maps between homology modules, and each exactness assertion reads elementwise as image $=$ kernel.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Acyclicity is inherited by the middle term]\label{cor:mid}
If $H_i(X_1)=0$ and $H_i(X_3)=0$ then $H_i(X_2)=0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Take $x \in H_i(X_2)$; its image in $H_i(X_3)$ vanishes, so by exactness at $H_i(X_2)$ it comes from $H_i(X_1)=0$, whence $x = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The connecting map as an isomorphism]\label{cor:delta}
If $H_i(X_2) = 0$ and $H_j(X_2) = 0$ with $j$ following $i$, then $\delta : H_i(X_3)\to H_j(X_1)$ is bijective.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Injectivity: $\delta(a-b)=0$ forces $a-b$ to lift to $H_i(X_2)=0$. Surjectivity: $w \in H_j(X_1)$ maps to $0$ in $H_j(X_2)=0$, hence lies in $\image\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:inj}
If $H_k(X_3)=0$ for the degree $k$ preceding $i$, then $H_i(f)$ is injective.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:surj}
If $H_j(X_1)=0$ for the degree $j$ following $i$, then $H_i(g)$ is surjective.
\end{corollary}

Applied to derived functors, Theorem~\ref{thm:les} yields the two long exact sequences for $\Ext$. For a short exact sequence $S: 0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ and fixed $Y$, $X$:
\[ \cdots\to\Ext^n(C,Y)\to\Ext^n(B,Y)\to\Ext^n(A,Y)\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon_S\circ-\ }\Ext^{n+1}(C,Y)\to\cdots \]
\[ \cdots\to\Ext^n(X,A)\to\Ext^n(X,B)\to\Ext^n(X,C)\xrightarrow{\ -\circ\varepsilon_S\ }\Ext^{n+1}(X,A)\to\cdots \]
In both cases the connecting map is Yoneda composition with the \emph{extension class} $\varepsilon_S \in \Ext^1(C,A)$. This concrete description makes the computations below possible in closed form. We also use the basic vanishing facts $\Ext^n(P,Y)=0$ for projective $P$ and $\Ext^n(X,I)=0$ for injective $I$, both for $n\ge 1$.

\section{Dimension bounds for $\Ext$}

\begin{theorem}[Projective dimension one for cyclic groups]\label{thm:extzmod}
Let $k\ne 0$, let $Y$ be any $\Z$-module and $n\ge 0$. Then $\Ext^{n+2}(\Z/k,Y)=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Apply the contravariant long exact sequence to $\mathcal{R}_k$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:freeres}), whose outer terms are projective:
\[ \Ext^{n+1}(\Z,Y)\longrightarrow\Ext^{n+2}(\Z/k,Y)\longrightarrow\Ext^{n+2}(\Z,Y). \]
Both ends vanish since $\Z$ is projective and $n+1,n+2\ge1$. Explicitly, for $x \in \Ext^{n+2}(\Z/k,Y)$ the restriction to $\Ext^{n+2}(\Z,Y)$ is zero, so $x = \varepsilon_{\mathcal{R}_k}\circ x_1$ with $x_1 \in \Ext^{n+1}(\Z,Y)=0$; hence $x=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Injective dimension one for $\Z$]\label{thm:extint}
For every $\Z$-module $X$ and every $n\ge0$, $\Ext^{n+2}(X,\Z)=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Dual argument with the covariant long exact sequence for $\mathcal{Q}$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:injres}). Given $x\in\Ext^{n+2}(X,\Z)$, exactness together with $\Ext^{n+1}(X,\Q)=\Ext^{n+2}(X,\Q)=0$ (as $\Q$ is injective) yields $x = x_3\circ\varepsilon_{\mathcal{Q}}$ with $x_3\in\Ext^{n+1}(X,\Q/\Z)=0$; hence $x=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Projective presentations with projective kernel]\label{thm:pp}
Let $0\to P_1\to P_0\to X\to 0$ be short exact with $P_0,P_1$ projective. Then $\Ext^{n+2}(X,Y)=0$ for every $Y$ and $n\ge0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Identical to Theorem~\ref{thm:extzmod}, with $\Z,\Z$ replaced by $P_1,P_0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Freeness of the kernel]\label{lem:freeker}
For any $n$, any $\Z$-module $X$ and any linear map $f:\Z^n\to X$, the kernel $\ker f$ is a free $\Z$-module.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$\ker f$ is a submodule of the finitely generated free module $\Z^n$ over the principal ideal domain $\Z$, and every such submodule is free of rank at most $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:kerses}
For a surjective linear map $f : M \to X$, the sequence $0\to\ker f\hookrightarrow M\xrightarrow{f}X\to0$ is short exact.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing for finitely generated groups]\label{thm:extfg}
Let $X$ be a finitely generated $\Z$-module and $Y$ any $\Z$-module. Then $\Ext^{n+2}(X,Y)=0$ for all $n\ge0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Pick generators $x_1,\dots,x_m$ of $X$ and let $f:\Z^m\to X$ send the $i$-th basis vector to $x_i$; its image is the submodule generated by the $x_i$, namely all of $X$, so $f$ is surjective. By Lemma~\ref{lem:kerses} the sequence $0\to\ker f\to\Z^m\to X\to0$ is short exact; by Lemma~\ref{lem:freeker} $\ker f$ is free, hence projective, and $\Z^m$ is projective. Theorem~\ref{thm:pp} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:hered}
The conclusion holds for \emph{all} abelian groups $X$: $\Z$ is hereditary, so any subgroup of any free abelian group is free, and the same two-step argument applies once the transfinite freeness theorem is available. The three cases established here --- $X$ cyclic, $Y=\Z$, $X$ finitely generated --- cover all cases arising in practice.
\end{remark}

\section{Computation of $\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)$}

Fix $k\ne0$ and a $\Z$-module $Y$, and let $\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\mathcal{R}_k}\in\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Z)$ be the class of the resolution $\mathcal{R}_k$.

\begin{definition}
For $y \in Y$ let $u_y : \Z \to Y$ be the unique homomorphism with $u_y(1)=y$, i.e.\ $u_y(n)=ny$. Define
\[ \Phi_Y : Y \longrightarrow \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y), \qquad \Phi_Y(y) := \varepsilon\circ u_y, \]
the pushforward of the extension class along $u_y$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:phihom}
$\Phi_Y$ is a homomorphism of abelian groups.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$u_{y+z} = u_y + u_z$, and both Yoneda composition and the passage from a morphism to its degree-zero $\Ext$-class are additive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Surjectivity]\label{thm:phisurj}
$\Phi_Y : Y \to \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)$ is surjective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $x \in \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)$. In degree $1$ the contravariant long exact sequence of $\mathcal{R}_k$ reads
\[ \Ext^0(\Z,Y)\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\circ-\ }\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)\longrightarrow\Ext^1(\Z,Y)=0, \]
the right-hand group vanishing as $\Z$ is projective. Exactness gives $x_1 \in \Ext^0(\Z,Y)=\Hom(\Z,Y)$ with $x = \varepsilon\circ x_1$. Every such homomorphism is $u_y$ for $y = x_1(1)$, so $x = \Phi_Y(y)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The kernel]\label{thm:phiker}
For $y \in Y$ we have $\Phi_Y(y)=0$ if and only if $y \in kY$; that is, $\ker\Phi_Y = kY$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) If $y = kz$ then $\mu_k\circ u_z = u_{kz} = u_y$, since $(\mu_k\circ u_z)(1) = u_z(k) = kz$. Hence $\Phi_Y(y) = \varepsilon\circ\mu_k\circ u_z$, and $\varepsilon\circ\mu_k = 0$ because two consecutive maps of the long exact sequence compose to zero.

($\Rightarrow$) If $\varepsilon\circ u_y = 0$, the relevant portion of the long exact sequence is
\[ \Ext^0(\Z,Y)\xrightarrow{\ \mu_k^*\ }\Ext^0(\Z,Y)\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\circ-\ }\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y), \]
with $\mu_k^*$ precomposition with $\mu_k$. Exactness at the middle spot gives $x_2 \in \Hom(\Z,Y)$ with $x_2\circ\mu_k = u_y$. Evaluating at $1$ yields $y = x_2(k) = k\,x_2(1)$, so $z := x_2(1)$ works.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$\Ext^1$ out of a cyclic group]\label{thm:extone}
For $k \neq 0$ and any $\Z$-module $Y$ there is an isomorphism of abelian groups
\[ Y/kY \;\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\; \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y), \qquad y+kY \longmapsto \varepsilon\circ u_y. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Combine Lemma~\ref{lem:phihom}, Theorem~\ref{thm:phisurj} and Theorem~\ref{thm:phiker} with the first isomorphism theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[$\Ext$ detects divisibility]\label{cor:div}
For $k\ne0$, $\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)=0$ if and only if $Y$ is $k$-divisible.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:extq}
$\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Q)=0$ for every $k\ne0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$\Q$ is $k$-divisible, since $q = k\cdot(q/k)$; apply Corollary~\ref{cor:div}. Equivalently $\Q/k\Q=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:extz}
For $k\ge2$, $\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Z)\cong\Z/k\ne0$; in particular the extension $0\to\Z\xrightarrow{\mu_k}\Z\to\Z/k\to0$ does not split.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:extone} gives $\Ext^1(\Z/k,\Z)\cong\Z/k\Z=\Z/k$. Directly: if every class vanished, Theorem~\ref{thm:phiker} applied to $y=1$ would give $z\in\Z$ with $kz=1$, hence $k\mid 1$ and $k\le1$, contradicting $k\ge2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:extclassif}
$\Ext^1(C,A)$ classifies extensions $0\to A\to B\to C\to0$ up to equivalence, the zero class being the split extension $B=A\oplus C$. Corollary~\ref{cor:extq} therefore says every extension of $\Z/k$ by $\Q$ splits; Corollary~\ref{cor:extz} says there are exactly $k$ inequivalent extensions of $\Z/k$ by $\Z$, only one of them split.
\end{remark}

\section{$\Tor$, torsion, and flatness}

\subsection{Degree zero and flat vanishing}
Let $R$ be commutative; $\Tor_n^R(G,-)$ is the $n$-th left derived functor of $G\otimes_R-$.

\begin{theorem}[Degree zero]\label{thm:torzero}
For all $R$-modules $G,M$ there is a natural isomorphism $\Tor_0^R(G,M)\cong G\otimes_R M$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The zeroth left derived functor of a right exact functor is the functor itself: if $P_1\to P_0\to M\to0$ is the tail of a projective resolution, right exactness gives $G\otimes P_1\to G\otimes P_0\to G\otimes M\to0$ exact, so $H_0(G\otimes P_\bullet)=\coker(G\otimes P_1\to G\otimes P_0)\cong G\otimes M$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Higher $\Tor$ against a flat module vanishes]\label{thm:torflat}
If $G$ is a flat $R$-module then $\Tor_{n+1}^R(G,M)=0$ for every $M$ and every $n\ge0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose a projective resolution $P_\bullet \to M$, so $\Tor_{n+1}(G,M) = H_{n+1}(G\otimes P_\bullet)$. Flatness makes $G\otimes-$ exact, and exact functors commute with homology, so $H_{n+1}(G\otimes P_\bullet)\cong G\otimes H_{n+1}(P_\bullet)$. A resolution is exact in positive degrees, so $H_{n+1}(P_\bullet)=0$ and the group is $G\otimes 0 = 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:notflat}
If $\Tor_{n+1}^R(G,M)\ne0$ for some $n\ge0$ and some $M$, then $G$ is not flat.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:torQZ}
Over $\Z$, $\Tor_{n+1}(\Q,M)=0$ and $\Tor_{n+1}(\Z,M)=0$ for every $M$ and $n\ge0$, since $\Q$ and $\Z$ are torsion-free, hence flat.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Higher $\Tor$ against a cyclic group]\label{thm:torvanish}
For $k\ne0$, every $\Z$-module $G$ and every $n\ge0$, $\Tor_{n+2}(G,\Z/k)=0$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$\Tor_{n+2}(G,\Z/k) = H_{n+2}(G\otimes C^{(k)})$ and $C^{(k)}_{n+2}=0$. More generally $(L_{n+2}F)(\Z/k)=0$ for any additive $F$, by Remark~\ref{rem:lengthone}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The first $\Tor$ group against a cyclic group}

\begin{theorem}[$\Tor$ is torsion]\label{thm:tortorsion}
Let $k\ne0$ and let $G$ be any $\Z$-module. Then
\[ \Tor_1(G,\Z/k) \;\cong\; G[k] = \ker(k\cdot : G\to G), \qquad G\otimes\Z/k \;\cong\; G/kG. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Compute along $C^{(k)}$. Tensoring gives $\cdots\to0\to G\otimes\Z\xrightarrow{1_G\otimes\mu_k}G\otimes\Z$ in degrees $1,0$. The right unitor $G\otimes\Z\cong G$ identifies $1_G\otimes\mu_k$ with multiplication by $k$ on $G$. The differential entering degree $1$ is zero (the complex vanishes in degree $2$), so
\[ \Tor_1(G,\Z/k) = \ker(1_G\otimes\mu_k)\cong\ker(k\cdot)=G[k]. \]
In degree zero the outgoing differential is zero, so the homology is the cokernel of the incoming one, $\coker(1_G\otimes\mu_k)\cong G/kG$, in agreement with Theorem~\ref{thm:torzero}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:torself}
For $k\ge2$, $\Tor_1(\Z/k,\Z/k)\cong(\Z/k)[k]=\Z/k\ne0$, since multiplication by $k$ is identically zero on $\Z/k$.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The flatness criterion}

\begin{theorem}[Five equivalent formulations of flatness over $\Z$]\label{thm:flat}
For an abelian group $G$ the following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $G$ is a flat $\Z$-module;
\item $G$ is torsion-free: $kg = 0$ with $k\ne0$ implies $g=0$;
\item $\ker(k\cdot:G\to G)=0$ for every $k\ne0$;
\item $\Tor_1(G,\Z/k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$;
\item $\Tor_{n+1}(G,M)=0$ for every $n\ge0$ and every $\Z$-module $M$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(2)$\Leftrightarrow$(3) is a restatement. (3)$\Leftrightarrow$(4) is Theorem~\ref{thm:tortorsion}. (1)$\Rightarrow$(5) is Theorem~\ref{thm:torflat}, and (5)$\Rightarrow$(4) is the case $n=0$, $M=\Z/k$. For (2)$\Rightarrow$(1): over a B\'ezout domain, in particular over the PID $\Z$, a module is flat exactly when its torsion submodule is trivial; torsion-freeness says every nonzero integer acts injectively, i.e.\ is a regular element on $G$. (For an arbitrary nonzero integer $r$ one replaces $r$ by $|r|$, which acts by $\pm$ the same map and has the same kernel.)
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:zmodnotflat}
For $k\ge2$, $\Z/k$ is not flat.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$k\cdot1=0$ in $\Z/k$ with $1\ne0$, so $\Z/k$ has torsion. Alternatively, $\Tor_1(\Z/k,\Z/k)\cong\Z/k\ne0$ and Corollary~\ref{cor:notflat}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Duality of the two computations]\label{rem:duality}
Theorems~\ref{thm:extone} and \ref{thm:tortorsion} are mirror images:
\[ \Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)\cong Y/kY,\qquad \Tor_1(G,\Z/k)\cong G[k], \]
with degree-zero counterparts $\Hom(\Z/k,Y)\cong Y[k]$ and $G\otimes\Z/k\cong G/kG$. Passing from degree $0$ to degree $1$ interchanges ``sub'' and ``quotient''. Both pairs come from the same two-term resolution, read in opposite directions.
\end{remark}

\section{Universal coefficients}

\subsection{Flat coefficients: no correction term}

\begin{theorem}[Universal coefficient theorem, flat case]\label{thm:uctflat}
Let $R$ be commutative, $G$ a flat $R$-module, $c$ an arbitrary complex shape and $K$ any complex of $R$-modules of shape $c$. Then for every degree $n$,
\[ H_n(G\otimes_R K)\;\cong\;G\otimes_R H_n(K), \]
by an $R$-linear isomorphism induced by the canonical comparison map.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Flatness makes $G\otimes_R-$ exact, and an exact additive functor commutes with the formation of homology of a short complex, since it preserves kernels, cokernels and images. Apply this at the short complex $K_{n+1}\to K_n\to K_{n-1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:flatacyclic}
If $G$ is flat and $H_n(K)=0$, then $H_n(G\otimes K)=0$.
\end{corollary}

Theorem~\ref{thm:uctflat} explains why homology with rational, real, or any torsion-free coefficients is so much simpler than integral homology: the correction term of the general universal coefficient sequence is then identically zero.

\subsection{Non-flat coefficients: the correction term is real}

For general $G$ the universal coefficient theorem asserts a natural short exact sequence
\[ 0\longrightarrow G\otimes H_n(C)\longrightarrow H_n(G\otimes C)\longrightarrow\Tor_1(G,H_{n-1}(C))\longrightarrow0 \]
for a complex $C$ of free modules. We exhibit both extreme cases in one minimal example. Let $k\ne0$ and $C = C^{(k)}$, so $H_0(C)\cong\Z/k$ and $H_n(C)=0$ for $n\ge1$.

\begin{theorem}[Degree zero: the tensor term alone]\label{thm:uctzero}
For every $\Z$-module $G$ and $k\ne0$,
\[ H_0(G\otimes C^{(k)})\;\cong\;G\otimes H_0(C^{(k)})\;\cong\;G/kG. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
There is no homology in degree $-1$, so the correction term is absent. Formally, $C^{(k)}$ is a projective resolution of $\Z/k$, so $H_0(G\otimes C^{(k)}) = \Tor_0(G,\Z/k)\cong G\otimes\Z/k$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:torzero}, and $\Z/k\cong H_0(C^{(k)})$. Identification with $G/kG$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:tortorsion}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Degree one: the correction term alone]\label{thm:uctone}
For every $\Z$-module $G$ and $k\ne0$,
\[ H_1(G\otimes C^{(k)})\;\cong\;\Tor_1\big(G,H_0(C^{(k)})\big)\;\cong\;G[k]. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $H_1(C^{(k)})=0$ the tensor term vanishes and the whole group is the correction term. Formally, $C^{(k)}$ is a projective resolution of $\Z/k\cong H_0(C^{(k)})$, so by definition $H_1(G\otimes C^{(k)}) = \Tor_1(G,\Z/k) \cong G[k]$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tortorsion}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Failure of exactness for non-flat coefficients]\label{thm:fail}
Let $k\ge2$. The short complex $0\to\Z\xrightarrow{\mu_k}\Z$ is exact, i.e.\ $H_1(C^{(k)})=0$, but its image under $-\otimes\Z/k$ is not exact: the class of $1\otimes1$ is a nonzero cycle that is not a boundary. Equivalently,
\[ H_1\big(\Z/k\otimes C^{(k)}\big)\cong\Tor_1(\Z/k,\Z/k)\cong\Z/k\ne0. \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Multiplication by $k$ is injective on $\Z$, so $H_1(C^{(k)})=0$. After tensoring with $\Z/k$ the differential becomes multiplication by $k$ on $\Z/k\otimes\Z\cong\Z/k$, which is the zero map; thus $1\otimes1$ is a cycle. There is nothing in degree $2$, so it is a boundary only if zero, and under $\Z/k\otimes\Z\cong\Z/k$ it corresponds to $1\ne0$ in $\Z/k$ (as $k\ge2$). Identification of the homology with $\Tor_1(\Z/k,\Z/k)\cong\Z/k$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:uctone} with Corollary~\ref{cor:torself}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:rp2}
Theorem~\ref{thm:fail} is the precise sense in which the correction term is not removable. The smallest topological illustration is the real projective plane $\RP^2$, whose integral homology is $H_0=\Z$, $H_1=\Z/2$, $H_2=0$: with $G=\Z/2$ the universal coefficient sequence gives $H_2(\RP^2;\Z/2)\cong\Tor_1(\Z/2,\Z/2)\cong\Z/2$, a top-degree class with no integral counterpart, produced entirely by the $\Tor$ term.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\subsection{Smith normal form and homology of a finitely generated complex}
Given a chain complex of finitely generated free abelian groups with integer boundary matrices $\partial_n$, put each into Smith normal form $U\partial_n V = \operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_r,0,\dots,0)$ with $d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_r$ and $U,V\in\mathrm{GL}(\Z)$. Then
\[ H_n\;\cong\;\Z^{\,\dim\ker\partial_n-\rank\partial_{n+1}}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r_{n+1}}\Z/d^{(n+1)}_i, \]
where the $d^{(n+1)}_i$ are the nontrivial elementary divisors of $\partial_{n+1}$. The reduction costs $O(mn\min(m,n))$ ring operations in naive form, with coefficient growth controlled by modular or fraction-free variants.

\subsection{$\Ext$ and $\Tor$ by elementary divisors}
Every finitely generated abelian group is $\Z^r\oplus\bigoplus_i\Z/a_i$; additivity of $\Ext$ and $\Tor$ in each variable reduces all computations to cyclic summands, where the table below is complete.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
 & degree $0$ & degree $1$ \\
\midrule
$\Ext^\bullet(\Z,Y)$ & $Y$ & $0$ \\
$\Ext^\bullet(\Z/a,\Z)$ & $0$ & $\Z/a$ \\
$\Ext^\bullet(\Z/a,\Z/b)$ & $\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ & $\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ \\
$\Tor_\bullet(\Z,M)$ & $M$ & $0$ \\
$\Tor_\bullet(\Z/a,\Z)$ & $\Z/a$ & $0$ \\
$\Tor_\bullet(\Z/a,\Z/b)$ & $\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ & $\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Indeed $\Ext^1(\Z/a,\Z/b)\cong(\Z/b)/a(\Z/b)\cong\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:extone}, and $\Tor_1(\Z/b,\Z/a)\cong(\Z/b)[a]\cong\Z/\gcd(a,b)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:tortorsion}; all degrees $\ge2$ vanish by Theorems~\ref{thm:extfg} and \ref{thm:torvanish}. Cost: one gcd per summand pair, $O(\log\min(a,b))$ each.

\subsection{Universal coefficients for a finitely generated complex}
Given $H_n\cong\Z^{r_n}\oplus\bigoplus_i\Z/a^{(n)}_i$ and $G\cong\Z^{s}\oplus\bigoplus_j\Z/b_j$, the universal coefficient sequence gives, non-canonically split for complexes of free modules,
\[ H_n(C;G)\;\cong\;\big(G\otimes H_n\big)\oplus\Tor_1\big(G,H_{n-1}\big), \]
computed summandwise from the table above. If $G$ is torsion-free the second term disappears, by Theorem~\ref{thm:uctflat}.

\section{Applications and discussion}

\textbf{Topology.} The universal coefficient theorem translates between integral homology and homology with arbitrary coefficients. Theorem~\ref{thm:uctflat} explains the simplification in the rational case: rational homology is the torsion-free shadow of integral homology, and Betti numbers are all one can see. Theorem~\ref{thm:fail} explains why mod-$p$ homology sees strictly more: the $\Tor$ term promotes $p$-torsion in $H_{n-1}$ to a genuine class in $H_n(-;\Z/p)$, as in Remark~\ref{rem:rp2}.

\textbf{Group theory.} By Remark~\ref{rem:extclassif}, $\Ext^1(C,A)$ classifies abelian extensions. Corollary~\ref{cor:extq} says $\Q$ absorbs cyclic quotients trivially; Corollary~\ref{cor:extz} gives exactly $k$ inequivalent extensions of $\Z/k$ by $\Z$. More generally Theorem~\ref{thm:extone} parametrises extensions of $\Z/k$ by $Y$ by $Y/kY$, an explicit finite computation whenever $Y$ is finitely generated.

\textbf{Commutative algebra.} Theorem~\ref{thm:flat} is the archetype of a homological characterisation of a ring-theoretic property: an infinite condition (exactness against all injections) collapses to $\Tor$ computations against cyclic modules. The general form is the criterion ``$\Tor_1^R(G,R/I)=0$ for all finitely generated ideals $I$'', of which (1)$\Leftrightarrow$(4) is the case $R=\Z$, where every ideal is $k\Z$.

\textbf{The hereditary phenomenon.} Theorems~\ref{thm:extzmod}, \ref{thm:extint}, \ref{thm:extfg} and \ref{thm:torvanish} all say the same thing from different angles: over $\Z$ the derived functors live in degrees $0$ and $1$ only. This is the defining property of a hereditary ring (global dimension $\le1$), which for a commutative domain means a Dedekind domain. Everything here generalises verbatim to Dedekind domains, with $\Z/k$ replaced by $R/\mathfrak{a}$ and ``$k$-divisible'' by ``$\mathfrak{a}$-divisible''.

\textbf{What is genuinely explicit.} The isomorphism $\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)\cong Y/kY$ is obtained not by a dimension count but from the named surjection $y\mapsto\varepsilon\circ u_y$ whose kernel is computed exactly, so one can point at a specific extension realising any given class. And the two-term complex $C^{(k)}$ isolates the two extreme cases of the universal coefficient sequence in one object: degree $0$ pure tensor, degree $1$ pure $\Tor$ --- the shortest possible proof that the correction term is unavoidable.

\textbf{Limitations.} Theorem~\ref{thm:extfg} covers finitely generated $X$; the fully general statement requires freeness of arbitrary subgroups of free abelian groups (Remark~\ref{rem:hered}). Theorems~\ref{thm:uctzero} and \ref{thm:uctone} establish the two extreme cases for the specific complex $C^{(k)}$; the full short exact sequence for an arbitrary complex of free modules is a natural next target.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Naturality of the degree-one computation.} Show that $\Ext^1(\Z/k,Y)\cong Y/kY$ is natural in $Y$: for every $f:Y\to Y'$ the square formed by the two isomorphisms, $\Ext^1(\Z/k,f)$, and the induced map $Y/kY\to Y'/kY'$ commutes.
\item \textbf{Full hereditarity.} Prove $\Ext^{n+2}(X,Y)=0$ for \emph{all} abelian groups, removing the finite generation hypothesis, via freeness of arbitrary subgroups of free abelian groups.
\item \textbf{The general universal coefficient sequence.} Construct $0\to G\otimes H_n(C)\to H_n(G\otimes C)\to\Tor_1(G,H_{n-1}(C))\to0$ for an arbitrary complex of free modules, prove it splits non-canonically, and establish naturality.
\item \textbf{K\"unneth.} Establish $0\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_p(C)\otimes H_q(D)\to H_n(C\otimes D)\to\bigoplus_{p+q=n-1}\Tor_1(H_p(C),H_q(D))\to0$, of which the universal coefficient theorem is the case where $D$ is concentrated in degree zero.
\item \textbf{Cohomological universal coefficients.} The dual sequence $0\to\Ext^1(H_{n-1}(C),G)\to H^n(C;G)\to\Hom(H_n(C),G)\to0$.
\item \textbf{Dedekind generalisations.} Reprove Sections 4--7 over an arbitrary Dedekind domain, covering rings of integers in number fields and coordinate rings of smooth affine curves.
\item \textbf{Beyond dimension one.} For a ring of global dimension $d>1$, such as $K[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ with the Koszul complex in place of $C^{(k)}$, compute the full tower $\Ext^0,\dots,\Ext^d$ against the residue field and observe the Betti numbers $\binom{d}{n}$.
\end{enumerate}

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import gcd
from typing import Iterable, Sequence

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Finitely generated abelian groups as multisets of invariants.
#   0 denotes a free Z summand;  a > 1 denotes a Z/a summand.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Group = tuple[int, ...]

Z: Group = (0,)
TRIVIAL: Group = ()


def zmod(k: int) -> Group:
    """The cyclic group Z/k (with Z/0 = Z, Z/1 = 0)."""
    if k == 0:
        return (0,)
    if k == 1:
        return ()
    return (k,)


def normalize(g: Iterable[int]) -> Group:
    """Drop trivial summands and sort, for canonical comparison."""
    return tuple(sorted(x for x in g if x != 1))


def group_str(g: Group) -> str:
    if not g:
        return "0"
    parts = ["Z" if x == 0 else f"Z/{x}" for x in sorted(g)]
    return " + ".join(parts)


def order(g: Group) -> int | None:
    """Order of a finite group, or None if it has a free summand."""
    n = 1
    for x in g:
        if x == 0:
            return None
        n *= x
    return n


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The complete degree-0 / degree-1 table for cyclic summands.
#
#   Hom(Z/a, Z/b)   = Z/gcd(a,b)        Ext^1(Z/a, Z/b) = Z/gcd(a,b)
#   Hom(Z/a, Z)     = 0                 Ext^1(Z/a, Z)   = Z/a
#   Hom(Z, Y)       = Y                 Ext^1(Z, Y)     = 0
#   (Z/a) (x) (Z/b) = Z/gcd(a,b)        Tor_1(Z/a,Z/b)  = Z/gcd(a,b)
#   (Z/a) (x) Z     = Z/a               Tor_1(Z/a, Z)   = 0
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def hom_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Hom(Z/a, Z/b) with the convention Z/0 = Z."""
    if a == 0:
        return zmod(b)
    if b == 0:
        return TRIVIAL
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def ext1_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Ext^1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b),  by  Ext^1(Z/k, Y) = Y/kY."""
    if a == 0:
        return TRIVIAL          # Z is projective
    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)          # Z / aZ
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def tensor_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """(Z/a) (x) (Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b)."""
    if a == 0:
        return zmod(b)
    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def tor1_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Tor_1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/a)[b],  by  Tor_1(G, Z/k) = G[k]."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:
        return TRIVIAL          # Z is flat
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def _bilinear(x: Group, y: Group, cell) -> Group:
    """Extend a function on cyclic summands additively in both variables."""
    out: list[int] = []
    for a, b in product(x, y):
        out.extend(cell(a, b))
    return normalize(out)


def hom(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, hom_cyclic)


def ext1(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, ext1_cyclic)


def tensor(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, tensor_cyclic)


def tor1(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, tor1_cyclic)


def ext_n(x: Group, y: Group, n: int) -> Group:
    """Ext^n over Z:  Hom in degree 0, the table in degree 1, zero above."""
    if n == 0:
        return hom(x, y)
    if n == 1:
        return ext1(x, y)
    return TRIVIAL              # Theorems: Ext^{n+2} = 0 over Z


def tor_n(x: Group, y: Group, n: int) -> Group:
    if n == 0:
        return tensor(x, y)
    if n == 1:
        return tor1(x, y)
    return TRIVIAL              # Theorems: Tor_{n+2}(-, Z/k) = 0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Brute-force verification on finite groups: direct construction of
#   G[k] = {g : kg = 0}  and  G/kG,
# realised inside the concrete product-of-cyclics model.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def elements(g: Group) -> list[tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All elements of a finite group given by invariants (no free part)."""
    assert all(x > 0 for x in g), "group must be finite"
    return [tuple(t) for t in product(*(range(x) for x in g))]


def scale(g: Group, k: int, v: Sequence[int]) -> tuple[int, ...]:
    return tuple((k * vi) % m for vi, m in zip(v, g))


def torsion_subgroup_size(g: Group, k: int) -> int:
    """|G[k]| computed by exhaustive search."""
    zero = tuple(0 for _ in g)
    return sum(1 for v in elements(g) if scale(g, k, v) == zero)


def quotient_size(g: Group, k: int) -> int:
    """|G/kG| = |G| / |kG|, computed by exhaustive search."""
    total = order(g)
    assert total is not None
    image = {scale(g, k, v) for v in elements(g)}
    return total // len(image)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Smith normal form and homology of an integral chain complex.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Matrix = list[list[int]]


def smith_normal_form(matrix: Matrix) -> list[int]:
    """Return the list of nonzero elementary divisors d_1 | d_2 | ... | d_r."""
    a = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(a), (len(a[0]) if a else 0)
    divisors: list[int] = []
    t = 0
    while t < rows and t < cols:
        # find a pivot
        pivot = None
        for i in range(t, rows):
            for j in range(t, cols):
                if a[i][j] != 0:
                    pivot = (i, j)
                    break
            if pivot:
                break
        if pivot is None:
            break
        pi, pj = pivot
        a[t], a[pi] = a[pi], a[t]
        for row in a:
            row[t], row[pj] = row[pj], row[t]
        # clear the pivot row and column by integer row/column reduction
        done = False
        while not done:
            done = True
            for i in range(t + 1, rows):
                if a[i][t] != 0:
                    q = a[i][t] // a[t][t]
                    for j in range(t, cols):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[t][j]
                    if a[i][t] != 0:
                        a[t], a[i] = a[i], a[t]
                        done = False
            for j in range(t + 1, cols):
                if a[t][j] != 0:
                    q = a[t][j] // a[t][t]
                    for i in range(t, rows):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[i][t]
                    if a[t][j] != 0:
                        for i in range(t, rows):
                            a[i][t], a[i][j] = a[i][j], a[i][t]
                        done = False
        divisors.append(abs(a[t][t]))
        t += 1
    # enforce the divisibility chain d_1 | d_2 | ...
    for i in range(len(divisors)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(divisors)):
            if divisors[j] % divisors[i] != 0:
                g = gcd(divisors[i], divisors[j])
                l = divisors[i] * divisors[j] // g
                divisors[i], divisors[j] = g, l
    return divisors


def rank(matrix: Matrix) -> int:
    return len(smith_normal_form(matrix))


def homology_of_complex(ranks: Sequence[int], boundaries: dict[int, Matrix],
                        n: int) -> Group:
    """
    H_n of a complex of free groups.  `ranks[i]` is the rank of C_i and
    `boundaries[i]` is the matrix of d_i : C_i -> C_{i-1} (rows = C_{i-1}).
    """
    d_n = boundaries.get(n, [[0] * ranks[n] for _ in range(ranks[n - 1] if n else 0)])
    d_next = boundaries.get(n + 1)
    r_n = rank(d_n) if d_n and d_n[0:1] else 0
    kernel_dim = ranks[n] - r_n
    if d_next is None:
        return normalize([0] * kernel_dim)
    divs = smith_normal_form(d_next)
    free_rank = kernel_dim - len(divs)
    return normalize([0] * free_rank + [d for d in divs if d > 1])

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from math import gcd
from typing import Iterable, Sequence

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Finitely generated abelian groups as multisets of invariants.
#   0 denotes a free Z summand;  a > 1 denotes a Z/a summand.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Group = tuple[int, ...]

Z: Group = (0,)
TRIVIAL: Group = ()


def zmod(k: int) -> Group:
    """The cyclic group Z/k (with Z/0 = Z, Z/1 = 0)."""
    if k == 0:
        return (0,)
    if k == 1:
        return ()
    return (k,)


def normalize(g: Iterable[int]) -> Group:
    """Drop trivial summands and sort, for canonical comparison."""
    return tuple(sorted(x for x in g if x != 1))


def group_str(g: Group) -> str:
    if not g:
        return "0"
    parts = ["Z" if x == 0 else f"Z/{x}" for x in sorted(g)]
    return " + ".join(parts)


def order(g: Group) -> int | None:
    """Order of a finite group, or None if it has a free summand."""
    n = 1
    for x in g:
        if x == 0:
            return None
        n *= x
    return n


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The complete degree-0 / degree-1 table for cyclic summands.
#
#   Hom(Z/a, Z/b)   = Z/gcd(a,b)        Ext^1(Z/a, Z/b) = Z/gcd(a,b)
#   Hom(Z/a, Z)     = 0                 Ext^1(Z/a, Z)   = Z/a
#   Hom(Z, Y)       = Y                 Ext^1(Z, Y)     = 0
#   (Z/a) (x) (Z/b) = Z/gcd(a,b)        Tor_1(Z/a,Z/b)  = Z/gcd(a,b)
#   (Z/a) (x) Z     = Z/a               Tor_1(Z/a, Z)   = 0
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def hom_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Hom(Z/a, Z/b) with the convention Z/0 = Z."""
    if a == 0:
        return zmod(b)
    if b == 0:
        return TRIVIAL
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def ext1_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Ext^1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b),  by  Ext^1(Z/k, Y) = Y/kY."""
    if a == 0:
        return TRIVIAL          # Z is projective
    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)          # Z / aZ
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def tensor_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """(Z/a) (x) (Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b)."""
    if a == 0:
        return zmod(b)
    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def tor1_cyclic(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Tor_1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/a)[b],  by  Tor_1(G, Z/k) = G[k]."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:
        return TRIVIAL          # Z is flat
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def _bilinear(x: Group, y: Group, cell) -> Group:
    """Extend a function on cyclic summands additively in both variables."""
    out: list[int] = []
    for a, b in product(x, y):
        out.extend(cell(a, b))
    return normalize(out)


def hom(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, hom_cyclic)


def ext1(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, ext1_cyclic)


def tensor(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, tensor_cyclic)


def tor1(x: Group, y: Group) -> Group:
    return _bilinear(x, y, tor1_cyclic)


def ext_n(x: Group, y: Group, n: int) -> Group:
    """Ext^n over Z:  Hom in degree 0, the table in degree 1, zero above."""
    if n == 0:
        return hom(x, y)
    if n == 1:
        return ext1(x, y)
    return TRIVIAL              # Theorems: Ext^{n+2} = 0 over Z


def tor_n(x: Group, y: Group, n: int) -> Group:
    if n == 0:
        return tensor(x, y)
    if n == 1:
        return tor1(x, y)
    return TRIVIAL              # Theorems: Tor_{n+2}(-, Z/k) = 0


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Brute-force verification on finite groups: direct construction of
#   G[k] = {g : kg = 0}  and  G/kG,
# realised inside the concrete product-of-cyclics model.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def elements(g: Group) -> list[tuple[int, ...]]:
    """All elements of a finite group given by invariants (no free part)."""
    assert all(x > 0 for x in g), "group must be finite"
    return [tuple(t) for t in product(*(range(x) for x in g))]


def scale(g: Group, k: int, v: Sequence[int]) -> tuple[int, ...]:
    return tuple((k * vi) % m for vi, m in zip(v, g))


def torsion_subgroup_size(g: Group, k: int) -> int:
    """|G[k]| computed by exhaustive search."""
    zero = tuple(0 for _ in g)
    return sum(1 for v in elements(g) if scale(g, k, v) == zero)


def quotient_size(g: Group, k: int) -> int:
    """|G/kG| = |G| / |kG|, computed by exhaustive search."""
    total = order(g)
    assert total is not None
    image = {scale(g, k, v) for v in elements(g)}
    return total // len(image)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Smith normal form and homology of an integral chain complex.
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Matrix = list[list[int]]


def smith_normal_form(matrix: Matrix) -> list[int]:
    """Return the list of nonzero elementary divisors d_1 | d_2 | ... | d_r."""
    a = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows, cols = len(a), (len(a[0]) if a else 0)
    divisors: list[int] = []
    t = 0
    while t < rows and t < cols:
        # find a pivot
        pivot = None
        for i in range(t, rows):
            for j in range(t, cols):
                if a[i][j] != 0:
                    pivot = (i, j)
                    break
            if pivot:
                break
        if pivot is None:
            break
        pi, pj = pivot
        a[t], a[pi] = a[pi], a[t]
        for row in a:
            row[t], row[pj] = row[pj], row[t]
        # clear the pivot row and column by integer row/column reduction
        done = False
        while not done:
            done = True
            for i in range(t + 1, rows):
                if a[i][t] != 0:
                    q = a[i][t] // a[t][t]
                    for j in range(t, cols):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[t][j]
                    if a[i][t] != 0:
                        a[t], a[i] = a[i], a[t]
                        done = False
            for j in range(t + 1, cols):
                if a[t][j] != 0:
                    q = a[t][j] // a[t][t]
                    for i in range(t, rows):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[i][t]
                    if a[t][j] != 0:
                        for i in range(t, rows):
                            a[i][t], a[i][j] = a[i][j], a[i][t]
                        done = False
        divisors.append(abs(a[t][t]))
        t += 1
    # enforce the divisibility chain d_1 | d_2 | ...
    for i in range(len(divisors)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(divisors)):
            if divisors[j] % divisors[i] != 0:
                g = gcd(divisors[i], divisors[j])
                l = divisors[i] * divisors[j] // g
                divisors[i], divisors[j] = g, l
    return divisors


def rank(matrix: Matrix) -> int:
    return len(smith_normal_form(matrix))


def homology_of_complex(ranks: Sequence[int], boundaries: dict[int, Matrix],
                        n: int) -> Group:
    """
    H_n of a complex of free groups.  `ranks[i]` is the rank of C_i and
    `boundaries[i]` is the matrix of d_i : C_i -> C_{i-1} (rows = C_{i-1}).
    """
    d_n = boundaries.get(n, [[0] * ranks[n] for _ in range(ranks[n - 1] if n else 0)])
    d_next = boundaries.get(n + 1)
    r_n = rank(d_n) if d_n and d_n[0:1] else 0
    kernel_dim = ranks[n] - r_n
    if d_next is None:
        return normalize([0] * kernel_dim)
    divs = smith_normal_form(d_next)
    free_rank = kernel_dim - len(divs)
    return normalize([0] * free_rank + [d for d in divs if d > 1])

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd

Matrix = list[list[int]]


def smith_normal_form(matrix: Matrix) -> list[int]:
    """Return the elementary divisors e_1 | e_2 | ... | e_r of `matrix`.

    Implements integer Gaussian elimination with the Euclidean pivoting rule:
    repeatedly reduce the pivot row and column modulo the pivot, swapping the
    pivot with any smaller nonzero remainder, until both are cleared.  Each
    pivot stage strictly decreases |pivot|, so the loop terminates.

    Complexity: O(m n min(m, n)) integer operations; entry growth is bounded
    in practice by the Euclidean reduction, and can be controlled rigorously
    by modular or fraction-free variants.
    """
    a = [row[:] for row in matrix]
    rows = len(a)
    cols = len(a[0]) if rows else 0
    divisors: list[int] = []
    t = 0
    while t < rows and t < cols:
        pivot: tuple[int, int] | None = None
        for i in range(t, rows):
            for j in range(t, cols):
                if a[i][j] != 0:
                    pivot = (i, j)
                    break
            if pivot is not None:
                break
        if pivot is None:
            break
        pi, pj = pivot
        a[t], a[pi] = a[pi], a[t]
        for row in a:
            row[t], row[pj] = row[pj], row[t]

        cleared = False
        while not cleared:
            cleared = True
            for i in range(t + 1, rows):
                if a[i][t] != 0:
                    q = a[i][t] // a[t][t]
                    for j in range(t, cols):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[t][j]
                    if a[i][t] != 0:
                        a[t], a[i] = a[i], a[t]
                        cleared = False
            for j in range(t + 1, cols):
                if a[t][j] != 0:
                    q = a[t][j] // a[t][t]
                    for i in range(t, rows):
                        a[i][j] -= q * a[i][t]
                    if a[t][j] != 0:
                        for i in range(t, rows):
                            a[i][t], a[i][j] = a[i][j], a[i][t]
                        cleared = False
        divisors.append(abs(a[t][t]))
        t += 1

    # enforce the divisibility chain e_1 | e_2 | ... | e_r
    for i in range(len(divisors)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(divisors)):
            if divisors[j] % divisors[i]:
                g = gcd(divisors[i], divisors[j])
                divisors[i], divisors[j] = g, divisors[i] * divisors[j] // g
    return divisors


def integral_rank(matrix: Matrix) -> int:
    """Rank over Z (equivalently over Q) via the number of elementary divisors."""
    return len(smith_normal_form(matrix))


def homology(ranks: dict[int, int], boundary: dict[int, Matrix],
             n: int) -> tuple[int, list[int]]:
    """Return (free rank of H_n, torsion invariants of H_n).

    `ranks[n]` is the rank of C_n; `boundary[n]` is the matrix of
    d_n : C_n -> C_{n-1}, with rows indexed by a basis of C_{n-1}.
    Missing entries are treated as zero modules / zero maps.
    """
    c_n = ranks.get(n, 0)
    r_out = integral_rank(boundary[n]) if n in boundary and c_n else 0
    kernel_dim = c_n - r_out
    divisors = smith_normal_form(boundary[n + 1]) if (n + 1) in boundary else []
    torsion = [e for e in divisors if e > 1]
    free_rank = kernel_dim - len(divisors)
    return free_rank, torsion


def pretty(free_rank: int, torsion: list[int]) -> str:
    parts: list[str] = []
    if free_rank == 1:
        parts.append("Z")
    elif free_rank > 1:
        parts.append(f"Z^{free_rank}")
    parts.extend(f"Z/{e}" for e in torsion)
    return " (+) ".join(parts) if parts else "0"

Group = tuple[int, ...]


def normalize(g: Iterable[int]) -> Group:
    return tuple(sorted(x for x in g if x != 1))

    return (0,) if k == 0 else (() if k == 1 else (k,))

    if not g:
        return "0"
    return " (+) ".join("Z" if x == 0 else f"Z/{x}" for x in sorted(g))

    """Hom(Z/a, Z/b), with Z/0 = Z."""

    """Ext^1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b)."""
    if a == 0:

    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))

    """(Z/a) (x) (Z/b) = (Z/b) / a(Z/b)."""
    if a == 0:
        return zmod(b)
    if b == 0:
        return zmod(a)
    return zmod(gcd(a, b))


def tor1_cell(a: int, b: int) -> Group:
    """Tor_1(Z/a, Z/b) = (Z/a)[b]."""
    if a == 0 or b == 0:

    return zmod(gcd(a, b))

    """Extend a cyclic-summand rule additively in both variables."""
    out: list[int] = []
    for a, b in product(x, y):
        out.extend(cell(a, b))
    return normalize(out)

    """Ext^n(X, Y) for finitely generated abelian groups over Z."""
    if n == 0:
        return bilinear(x, y, hom_cell)
    if n == 1:
        return bilinear(x, y, ext1_cell)
    return ()          # Z is hereditary

    """Tor_n(X, Y) for finitely generated abelian groups over Z."""
    if n == 0:
        return bilinear(x, y, tensor_cell)
    if n == 1:
        return bilinear(x, y, tor1_cell)
    return ()          # Z is hereditary


def is_flat(g: Group) -> bool:
    """G is flat  <=>  G is torsion-free  <=>  Tor_1(G, Z/k) = 0 for all k."""
    return all(x == 0 for x in g)

import numpy as np

Group = tuple[int, ...]        # 0 = free Z summand, a > 1 = Z/a summand


def tensor_order(g: Group, h: Group) -> int:
    """|G (x) H| for finite G, treating a free summand of H as contributing |G|."""
    total = 1
    for a in g:
        for b in h:
            if a == 0 and b == 0:
                return 0          # infinite; not used below
            if a == 0:
                total *= b
            elif b == 0:
                total *= a
            else:
                total *= gcd(a, b)
    return total


def tor_order(g: Group, h: Group) -> int:
    total = 1
    for a in g:
        for b in h:
            if a == 0 or b == 0:
                continue
            total *= gcd(a, b)
    return total

/* ---------- tiny abelian-group model: invariants, 0 = free Z ---------- */
const MODULES = {
  Z:    {inv:[0],   tex:"\\mathbb{Z}",                       divisible:false},
  Q:    {inv:"Q",   tex:"\\mathbb{Q}",                       divisible:true},
  C4:   {inv:[4],   tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/4",                     divisible:false},
  C6:   {inv:[6],   tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/6",                     divisible:false},
  C8:   {inv:[8],   tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/8",                     divisible:false},
  C9:   {inv:[9],   tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/9",                     divisible:false},
  C12:  {inv:[12],  tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/12",                    divisible:false},
  ZC2:  {inv:[0,2], tex:"\\mathbb{Z}\\oplus\\mathbb{Z}/2",   divisible:false},
  C2C3: {inv:[2,3], tex:"\\mathbb{Z}/2\\oplus\\mathbb{Z}/3", divisible:false}
};

const gcd = (a,b) => b ? gcd(b, a % b) : Math.abs(a);

function texOf(inv){
  if (inv === "Q") return "\\mathbb{Q}";
  const parts = inv.filter(x => x !== 1)
                   .map(x => x === 0 ? "\\mathbb{Z}" : `\\mathbb{Z}/${x}`);
  return parts.length ? parts.join(" \\oplus ") : "0";
}

/* Ext^1(Z/k, Y) = Y/kY   (summandwise: Z/kZ, (Z/b)/k = Z/gcd(k,b), Q/kQ = 0) */
function extOne(inv, k){
  if (inv === "Q") return [];
  return inv.map(b => b === 0 ? k : gcd(k,b)).filter(x => x !== 1);
}
/* Tor_1(G, Z/k) = G[k]   (summandwise: Z[k]=0, (Z/b)[k]=Z/gcd(k,b), Q[k]=0) */
function torOne(inv, k){
  if (inv === "Q") return [];
  return inv.map(b => b === 0 ? 1 : gcd(k,b)).filter(x => x !== 1);
}
/* G (x) Z/k = G/kG  -- same formula as Ext^1 above */
const tensorZk = extOne;

function orderOf(inv){
  if (inv === "Q") return Infinity;
  let n = 1;
  for (const x of inv){ if (x === 0) return Infinity; n *= x; }
  return n;
}

/* ---------- the resolution picture ---------- */
function drawResolution(k){
  const svg = document.getElementById("resSvg");
  const arrow = (x1,x2,y,label,colour) => `

          stroke="${colour}" stroke-width="2.2"/>
    <polygon points="${x2},${y} ${x2-13},${y-5.5} ${x2-13},${y+5.5}" fill="${colour}"/>
    <text x="${(x1+x2)/2}" y="${y-12}" fill="${colour}" font-size="15"
          text-anchor="middle" font-family="serif" font-style="italic">${label}</text>`;
  const node = (x,y,t,colour) => `
    <text x="${x}" y="${y+6}" fill="${colour}" font-size="24" text-anchor="middle"
          font-family="serif">${t}</text>`;
  svg.innerHTML = `
    <rect width="900" height="150" fill="none"/>
    ${node(60,55,"0","#94a3c4")}
    ${arrow(80,175,55,"","#94a3c4")}
    ${node(200,55,"\u2124","#7dd3fc")}
    ${arrow(225,345,55,"\u00b7"+k,"#7dd3fc")}
    ${node(370,55,"\u2124","#7dd3fc")}
    ${arrow(395,520,55,"mod "+k,"#4ade80")}
    ${node(560,55,"\u2124/"+k,"#4ade80")}
    ${arrow(600,700,55,"","#94a3c4")}
    ${node(725,55,"0","#94a3c4")}
    <text x="450" y="112" fill="#94a3c4" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">
      free (= projective) — the resolution stops here, so nothing survives in degree ≥ 2
    </text>
    <text x="450" y="134" fill="#94a3c4" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">
      dual picture: 0 → ℤ → ℚ → ℚ/ℤ → 0, an injective resolution of ℤ of the same length
    </text>`;
  document.getElementById("resNote").textContent =
    "Multiplication by " + k + " is injective on Z; reduction mod " + k +
    " is surjective; an integer reduces to 0 exactly when it is a multiple of " + k + ".";
}

/* ---------- chips ---------- */
function chipRow(el, items, cls){
  el.innerHTML = items.map(t => `<span class="chip ${cls}">${t}</span>`).join("");
}

/* ---------- main update ---------- */
function update(){
  const k = +document.getElementById("k").value;
  const key = document.getElementById("mod").value;
  const M = MODULES[key];
  document.getElementById("kv").textContent = k;
  drawResolution(k);

  const ext = extOne(M.inv, k);
  const tor = torOne(M.inv, k);
  const ten = tensorZk(M.inv, k);

  /* Ext panel */
  document.getElementById("extOut").innerHTML =

  const extZero = ext.length === 0;
  document.getElementById("extVerdict").innerHTML = extZero
    ? `<span class="verdict ok">vanishes</span> — the module is
       ${k}-divisible, so <em>every</em> extension of $\\mathbb{Z}/${k}$ by it splits.`
    : `<span class="verdict no">non-zero</span> — there are
       ${orderOf(ext) === Infinity ? "infinitely many" : orderOf(ext)}
       inequivalent extensions, only one of which splits.`;
  document.getElementById("extNote").innerHTML = extZero
    ? `Every element $y$ can be written $y = ${k}z$, so the surjection
       $y \\mapsto \\varepsilon\\circ u_y$ has all of $Y$ in its kernel.`
    : `The map $y \\mapsto \\varepsilon \\circ u_y$ is onto with kernel exactly
       $${k}Y$$, so the quotient $Y/${k}Y$ is the answer.`;

  const extOrd = orderOf(ext);
  if (extOrd === 0 || ext.length === 0){
    chipRow(document.getElementById("extChips"), ["0  (split only)"], "cool");
  } else if (extOrd !== Infinity && extOrd <= 40){

  "interactive_layout": "# Derived Functors over the Integers
### A guided tour of $\operatorname{Ext}$, $\operatorname{Tor}$, and the ghosts they leave behind

---

## 0. A subtraction problem that isn't

Multiply the integers by $2$. The map $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $n\mapsto 2n$, is **injective** — nothing is lost.

Now reduce everything modulo $2$, i.e. apply $-\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2$. The map becomes multiplication by $2$ on $\mathbb{Z}/2$, which is the **zero map**. Injectivity has evaporated.

Something was destroyed by an operation that only ever adds relations. Where did it go?

The answer is the whole subject: it became a group, $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/2,\mathbb{Z}/2)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$. This page is a guided tour of that idea and its twin.

<details>
<summary><strong>Prerequisites — click if "abelian group" and "exact sequence" are not yet second nature</strong></summary>

An **abelian group** is a set with a commutative, associative addition, a zero, and negatives — think $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, or the clock group $\mathbb{Z}/k$ of residues modulo $k$. Every abelian group is the same thing as a **module over the ring $\mathbb{Z}$**, and we use the two words interchangeably.

A sequence of homomorphisms $A \xrightarrow{f} B \xrightarrow{g} C$ is **exact at $B$** if $\operatorname{im} f = \ker g$: everything killed by $g$ comes from $A$, and nothing else. A **short exact sequence**
$$0 \to A \xrightarrow{f} B \xrightarrow{g} C \to 0$$
says exactly that $f$ is injective, $g$ is surjective, and $A$ sits inside $B$ as the kernel of $g$ — so $B$ is built out of $A$ and $C$. Such a $B$ is called an **extension of $C$ by $A$**; the boring one is $B = A \oplus C$, called the **split** extension.

The **tensor product** $A \otimes B$ is the universal receiver of bilinear maps out of $A\times B$. The only fact you need here: $A \otimes \mathbb{Z}/k \cong A/kA$, and $A \otimes \mathbb{Z} \cong A$. Further reading: [exact sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exact_sequence), [tensor product of modules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tensor_product_of_modules).
</details>

---

## 1. Good objects, and resolving bad ones

Some abelian groups are *good*.

- **Projective** ($=$ free, over $\mathbb{Z}$): so free of relations that any map into a quotient lifts. Examples: $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Z}^n$.
- **Injective** ($=$ divisible, over $\mathbb{Z}$): every element has an $n$-th multiple root, so maps *into* it always extend. Examples: $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$. Note $\mathbb{Z}$ is **not** injective — you cannot divide $1$ by $2$ inside $\mathbb{Z}$.
- **Flat**: tensoring with it destroys nothing. Over $\mathbb{Z}$ this turns out to mean *torsion-free*.

The bad object $\mathbb{Z}/k$ is none of these. But it can be **resolved** — written as the end of a short chain of good objects. The star of the story is the shortest resolution imaginable:

$$0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\;\cdot k\;} \mathbb{Z} \xrightarrow{\;\bmod k\;} \mathbb{Z}/k \longrightarrow 0 .$$

Its mirror image resolves $\mathbb{Z}$ by injectives:

$$0 \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q} \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} \longrightarrow 0 .$$

**Derived functors** are computed by a fixed recipe: throw away the object, keep the resolution, apply your functor, take homology. Degree $0$ gives back the original functor; the higher degrees are the correction terms.

The first widget is the laboratory where all of this becomes concrete. Move the slider and watch both closed formulas — $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,Y)\cong Y/kY$ and $\operatorname{Tor}_1(G,\mathbb{Z}/k)\cong G[k]$ — react in real time.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

> **Things worth trying.** Set the module to $\mathbb{Q}$: $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ collapses to zero for every $k$, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible. Set it to $\mathbb{Z}$: now $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/k$ is as big as it can be, and the extension $0\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/k\to 0$ is one of the $k-1$ non-split ones. Set it to $\mathbb{Z}/4$ and sweep $k$ through $2,4,8$: the answer is $\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(k,4)$ every time.

<details>
<summary><strong>Why the tower stops at degree one</strong></summary>

If a projective resolution $P_\bullet$ of $M$ has $P_n = 0$ for $n \geq 2$, then for any additive functor $F$,
$$(L_nF)(M) = H_n\big(F(P_\bullet)\big) = 0 \quad (n \geq 2),$$
simply because $F(0) = 0$: there is nothing left to take homology of. Dually for right derived functors and injective resolutions.

Since both of our resolutions have length one, we immediately get
$$\operatorname{Ext}^{n}(\mathbb{Z}/k, Y) = 0,\qquad \operatorname{Tor}_{n}(G,\mathbb{Z}/k)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Ext}^{n}(X,\mathbb{Z})=0 \qquad (n \geq 2).$$

This extends to *every finitely generated* $X$: pick a surjection $\mathbb{Z}^m\twoheadrightarrow X$; the kernel is a subgroup of a finitely generated free group over a principal ideal domain, hence itself free. So $X$ has a length-one free presentation, and $\operatorname{Ext}^{n}(X,Y)=0$ for all $n \geq 2$ and all $Y$. This is the property of $\mathbb{Z}$ known as being a [hereditary ring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hereditary_ring): homological algebra over $\mathbb{Z}$ is a two-storey building.
</details>

---

## 2. The engine room: the long exact sequence

Everything above is powered by one machine. Given a short exact sequence of complexes $0 \to C' \to C \to C'' \to 0$, homology is not exact — but the failure is perfectly organised into an infinite staircase:

$$\cdots \to H_n(C') \to H_n(C) \to H_n(C'') \xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} H_{n-1}(C') \to H_{n-1}(C) \to \cdots$$

exact at every spot. The connecting map $\partial$ is built by the diagram chase every algebraist learns once and never forgets.

<details>
<summary><strong>The snake, step by step</strong></summary>

Let $z$ be a cycle in $C''_n$, representing a class in $H_n(C'')$.

1. **Lift.** Since $C_n \to C''_n$ is surjective, pick $\tilde z \in C_n$ mapping to $z$.
2. **Differentiate.** Consider $d\tilde z \in C_{n-1}$. Its image in $C''_{n-1}$ is $dz = 0$.
3. **Descend.** By exactness, $d\tilde z = f(w)$ for a unique $w \in C'_{n-1}$.
4. **Check.** $f(dw) = d(d\tilde z) = 0$ and $f$ is injective, so $dw = 0$: $w$ is a cycle.
5. **Define.** $\partial[z] := [w]$.

Different choices of $\tilde z$ differ by something from $C'_n$, which changes $w$ by a boundary — so $[w]$ is well defined. Exactness at all three spots is three more chases in the same spirit.
</details>

Four consequences do all the practical work:

- if $C'$ and $C''$ are acyclic in degree $n$, so is $C$;
- if $C$ is acyclic in two adjacent degrees, $\partial$ is a **bijection**;
- if $H_{n-1}(C'')=0$ then $H_n(C')\to H_n(C)$ is injective;
- if $H_{n+1}(C')=0$ then $H_n(C)\to H_n(C'')$ is surjective.

For $\operatorname{Ext}$ there are two such staircases, one in each variable, and in both the connecting map is *composition with a single universal class*: the extension class $\varepsilon_S \in \operatorname{Ext}^1(C,A)$ of the sequence $S$. That concrete description is what makes the next section possible in closed form.

---

## 3. $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ is an obstruction group you can hold in your hand

Here is the complete answer for cyclic groups.

> **Theorem.** For $k \neq 0$ and any abelian group $Y$,
> $$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k, Y) \;\cong\; Y/kY .$$

And the isomorphism is *explicit*. Let $\varepsilon$ be the class of $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\cdot k}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/k\to 0$. Each $y \in Y$ gives a map $u_y:\mathbb{Z}\to Y$, $1 \mapsto y$; push $\varepsilon$ forward along it to get $\varepsilon\circ u_y$. This assignment is a homomorphism, it is onto, and its kernel is exactly $kY$.

<details>
<summary><strong>The two halves of the proof</strong></summary>

**Surjectivity.** In degree $1$ the long exact sequence of the resolution reads
$$\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},Y)\xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\circ-\ }\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,Y)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z},Y)=0,$$
the last group vanishing because $\mathbb{Z}$ is projective. So every class is $\varepsilon\circ x_1$ for some $x_1 \in \operatorname{Hom}(\mathbb{Z},Y)$, and every such $x_1$ is $u_y$ with $y = x_1(1)$.

**The kernel.** If $y = kz$, then $\mu_k \circ u_z = u_{kz} = u_y$, so $\varepsilon\circ u_y = (\varepsilon\circ\mu_k)\circ u_z = 0$, since two consecutive maps in an exact sequence compose to zero. Conversely, if $\varepsilon\circ u_y = 0$, exactness one step earlier gives $x_2$ with $x_2\circ\mu_k = u_y$; evaluating at $1$ yields $y = k\,x_2(1)$.

Now apply the first isomorphism theorem.
</details>

Two corollaries, both immediate and both memorable:

- **$\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k, Y) = 0$ if and only if $Y$ is $k$-divisible.**
- Hence $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,\mathbb{Q}) = 0$ — every extension of a cyclic group by $\mathbb{Q}$ splits — while $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/k,\mathbb{Z}) \cong \mathbb{Z}/k \neq 0$ for $k \geq 2$, because you cannot divide $1$ by $k$ inside $\mathbb{Z}$.

That last statement is worth pausing on: $\operatorname{Ext}^1$ has just detected, in the language of group extensions, the most elementary fact about the integers there is. See [Ext functor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext_functor) for the classification-of-extensions picture.

---

## 4. $\operatorname{Tor}$ is torsion, and flatness is a finite test

Dually:

> **Theorem.** For any abelian group $G$ and any $k$,
> $$\operatorname{Tor}_1(G,\mathbb{Z}/k) \;\cong\; G[k] = \{g : kg = 0\}, \qquad G \otimes \mathbb{Z}/k \;\cong\; G/kG .$$

There is the whole picture in one line: **$\operatorname{Tor}$ is called that because it *is* torsion.** Tensoring gives you the quotient $G/kG$; the correction term gives you the sub $G[k]$.

The payoff is a criterion that turns an infinite condition into a finite family of computations.

> **Theorem (flatness criterion).** For an abelian group $G$ the following are equivalent:
> (1) $G$ is flat; (2) $G$ is torsion-free; (3) multiplication by every $k\ne0$ is injective on $G$; (4) $\operatorname{Tor}_1(G,\mathbb{Z}/k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$; (5) $\operatorname{Tor}_n(G,M)=0$ for every $n\ge1$ and every $M$.

<details>
<summary><strong>How the cycle of implications closes</strong></summary>

(1) $\Rightarrow$ (5): tensoring with a flat module is exact, exact functors commute with homology, and a resolution has no homology in positive degrees. Nothing survives.

(5) $\Rightarrow$ (4): the special case $n=1$, $M = \mathbb{Z}/k$.

(4) $\Leftrightarrow$ (3): the computation $\operatorname{Tor}_1(G,\mathbb{Z}/k)\cong G[k]$ above.

(3) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2): a homomorphism has trivial kernel iff it is injective.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1): over the principal ideal domain $\mathbb{Z}$, a module is flat exactly when its torsion submodule is trivial.
</details>

And the punchline: $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/k,\mathbb{Z}/k)\cong\mathbb{Z}/k \neq 0$ for $k \geq 2$, so cyclic groups are precisely the standard non-flat examples — and $\operatorname{Tor}$ says exactly how badly they fail.

For cyclic groups everything reduces to a *single arithmetic function*. Both $\operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathbb{Z}/a,\mathbb{Z}/b)$ and $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/a,\mathbb{Z}/b)$ are $\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(a,b)$. Here is that landscape:

{{visualization:0}}

The white region on the right is the vanishing locus: coprime pairs, where nothing goes wrong. Its density tends to $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.6079$ — so a "random" pair of cyclic groups has about a $61\%$ chance of interacting trivially.

---

## 5. Universal coefficients: two layers of homology

Suppose you know the integral homology of a space and want its homology with coefficients in $G$: take the chain complex $C$, tensor with $G$, take homology. The naive hope is $H_n(G\otimes C)\cong G\otimes H_n(C)$.

> **Theorem (flat case).** If $G$ is flat, the hope is correct: $H_n(G\otimes C)\cong G\otimes H_n(C)$ in every degree, for every complex.

For non-flat $G$ the hope is false, and the failure is a measurement:

$$0 \longrightarrow G\otimes H_n(C) \longrightarrow H_n(G\otimes C) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Tor}_1\big(G, H_{n-1}(C)\big) \longrightarrow 0 .$$

Homology with coefficients has **two layers**: the expected part in degree $n$, and a ghost of degree $n-1$ that arrived via $\operatorname{Tor}$. The second widget is a machine for this: pick a space, pick coefficients, and watch the layers separate.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

> **Things worth trying.** $\mathbb{RP}^2$ with $\mathbb{Z}/2$ coefficients: a class appears in degree $2$ even though $H_2(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{Z})=0$. It is the $2$-torsion of $H_1$, resurfacing one degree up. Switch to $\mathbb{Z}/3$ coefficients and it vanishes — $\gcd(3,2)=1$. Switch to $\mathbb{Q}$ and *all* ghosts vanish at once, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is flat.

Here is the same phenomenon plotted across several spaces, together with the sharpest possible demonstration that the correction term is not optional:

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary><strong>The minimal counterexample, in full</strong></summary>

Let $C$ be the two-term complex $\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\cdot k}\mathbb{Z}$, so $H_0(C) = \mathbb{Z}/k$ and $H_1(C)=0$. Then for any $G$:

- **Degree $0$:** there is no homology in degree $-1$, so the correction term is absent and $H_0(G\otimes C)\cong G\otimes H_0(C)\cong G/kG$. *Pure tensor.*
- **Degree $1$:** $H_1(C)=0$, so the tensor term is absent and the entire group is the correction term: $H_1(G\otimes C)\cong \operatorname{Tor}_1(G,H_0(C))\cong G[k]$. *Pure ghost.*

Now take $G=\mathbb{Z}/k$ with $k\ge2$. The complex $C$ is exact in degree $1$ — multiplication by $k$ is injective on $\mathbb{Z}$. After tensoring, the differential is multiplication by $k$ on $\mathbb{Z}/k$, which is zero. So $1\otimes 1$ is a cycle, it is not a boundary, and it is not zero: exactness has been destroyed, and what survives is exactly $\operatorname{Tor}_1(\mathbb{Z}/k,\mathbb{Z}/k)\cong\mathbb{Z}/k$.

If you delete the correction term from the universal coefficient theorem, the theorem becomes false. This is the proof.
</details>

---

## 6. Computing it all

For finitely generated groups every statement above is effective. Three procedures suffice.

**(a) Homology of an integral complex** — reduce each boundary matrix to [Smith normal form](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smith_normal_form) and read off free ranks and elementary divisors.

{{algorithm:0}}

**(b) $\operatorname{Ext}$ and $\operatorname{Tor}$ by elementary divisors** — decompose into cyclic summands, apply the closed formulas summandwise, and take gcds.

{{algorithm:1}}

**(c) The universal coefficient algorithm** — combine (a) and (b): the two layers per degree, computed exactly.

{{algorithm:2}}

Put the three together and you can compute the homology of any finite complex with any finitely generated coefficient group, and split the answer into what was expected and what is a ghost.

Finally, a single script that walks through every result on this page — the resolutions, the two closed formulas cross-checked against exhaustive enumeration of finite groups, the flatness criterion, the universal coefficient computation, and the topological punchline.
